title: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite: when to pick each

videos.script: Eleven lessons of SQL, and almost none of it was about a product. That was deliberate. The relational model, the joins, the transactions, the indexes and the plan are the same subject whichever engine runs them. {{same}} This lesson is about the edges, where they stop being the same. There are four here. PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. {{four}} Start with the one that is not like the others. SQLite has no server. It is a library inside your program and a database that is one file, and that single fact decides almost everything about where it belongs. {{sqlite}} The other three are servers you connect to over a socket. MariaDB is a fork of MySQL from 2009, and after fifteen years apart they are two engines that mostly agree. {{servers}} Then the part you will actually trip over. The same INSERT is refused by one engine and accepted by another. The same WHERE on an e-mail address finds a row on one and nothing on the next. The same ALTER TABLE inside a transaction rolls back here and does not there. {{differ}} We will run all three of those and look at what comes back, because the differences are small to read and expensive to meet for the first time in production. {{run}} And at the end, the choice. Which is worth less than you think, because most of the time you do not make it. You join a company and the engine is already there. {{choose}}
